newsitem.title: UK: Who's in charge with Blair away? media asks.
newsitem.headline: Who's in charge with Blair away? media asks.

text.p: With Prime Minister Tony Blair on a family holiday in Tuscany, who is in charge of the British government?
Has deputy Prime Minister John Prescott, the blunt-speaking former ship's steward whose Yorkshire accent reminds the ruling Labour Party of its proletarian roots, duly taken over?

Or are the shots being called by Peter Mandelson, the smooth-talking Minister without Portfolio responsible for government policy coordination, whose efforts to win Labour favourable publicity played a vital part in the party's crushing May 1 election victory?
The questions have been picked over for the past week by Britain's newspapers, hungry for political tittle-tattle to fill their August pages.

Why, they asked, did Mandelson chair a news conference at which European Competitiveness Minister Lord David Simon announced he was selling the British Petroleum shares which had landed him at the centre of a storm over a potential conflict of interest?

Why last Friday did he appear alongside Prescott at another media event to celebrate Labour's first 100 days in office following its May 1 election victory, explaining that the two were "minding the shop" while Blair was in Italy?
On Monday, Prescott appeared to react to the suggestion that he was Blair's deputy in name only by conspicuously intervening in a visa dispute.

After hearing a feature on a BBC radio news programme about a group of trainee Asian and African priests who had been denied permission to visit Britain for a few weeks, Prescott telephoned the programme to say he would personally examine the case.
"It is just a question of looking at...whether there is a problem with coordination between government departments," a government spokesman said later.

Mandelson is well used to taunts that in his efforts to present his party in the best possible light he regularly browbeats journalists and monitors the public utterances of junior Labour parliamentarians to ensure they are "on message".
But questions about his role over the three weeks that Blair will spend with his wife Cherie and their three children in Italy appeared to get under his skin.
A reporter who asked him at Friday's news conference about his role was accused of asking "vainglorious, self-indulgent questions".
"The only people who are preoccupied with my role are preoccupied with it because they are preoccupied by themselves," Mandelson told the BBC reporter.
The BBC said that after broadcasting an interview with Mandelson on Friday, they received dozens of calls from listeners complaining about the tongue-lashing he gave his interviewer.
The opposition parties seized on Mandelson's ill-tempered replies, claiming they were signs of a politician who no longer considered himself answerable to the voters.
They pointed out that, in stark contrast to ministers with departmental responsibilities, Mandelson had not spoken, or answered questions, in parliament for a year.

"The king of media manipulation believes he is so important that he need only answer questions he has framed himself," said Francis Maude, the opposition Conservatives' spokesman on culture and the media.
"The Minister without Portfolio is rapidly becoming the minister without accountability."
